### App

File: `src/app/app.ts`
Selector: `app-root`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: Application shell: header, navigation, the language switch, the footer and the routed view.

Properties:
- `aiUsageUrl: unknown = AI_USAGE_URL`
- `auth: unknown = inject(AuthService)`
- `canModerate: unknown = computed( () => this.isAdmin() || this.auth.realmRoles().some((role) => role.toLowerCase() === 'schichtleiter'), )` — Whether to offer the protocol view — and it is two different views behind one entry. The admin reviews, approves and archives. The Schichtleiter corrects, and since 2026-08-14 reaches the same route to do it: they had held the correction endpoint alone since 2026-08-13 with no door onto it, so the permission existed and the path did not. Presentation, like canUpload — the route guard and, decisively, the backend decide. What it buys is that the two roles with a job here have a door and the two without one do not. What the door OPENS ONTO differs by role: the component renders the controls each may use, and nav.moderation is worded for the reader rather than for the route.
- `canSearch: unknown = computed(() => !this.isAdmin())` — Whether to offer the search view. Everyone but the admin, and that is the same defect the routing fixes seen from the header: an admin may not ask questions by decision, so the entry led to a view whose machine picker they are not allowed to fill. A nav entry onto an error message is worse than no nav entry.
- `canUpload: unknown = computed(() => this.auth.realmRoles().some((role) => role.toLowerCase() === 'schichtleiter'), )` — Whether to offer the upload view at all. Hiding the link is presentation, not protection — the route guard and, above all, the backend decide who may upload. What it buys is that the three roles who cannot upload are not shown a door that opens onto a 403.
- `docsUrl: unknown = DOCS_URL`
- `helpOpen: unknown = signal(false)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `isAdmin: unknown = computed(() => this.auth.realmRoles().some((role) => role.toLowerCase() === 'admin'), )` — The one role whose navigation differs in kind rather than in degree.
- `isAuthenticated: unknown = this.auth.isAuthenticated`
- `language: unknown = this.i18n.language`
- `moderationLabel: unknown = computed(() => this.isAdmin() ? this.t().nav.moderation : this.t().nav.corrections, )` — What to call that entry, because the two roles do not do the same thing behind it. "Protokollverwaltung" describes reviewing and removing; a Schichtleiter does neither. Naming the link after the job is part of what makes the trust chain legible from the screen — a corrector who clicks "Verwaltung" and finds no delete button has been told the wrong thing about their own role.
- `repoUrl: unknown = REPO_URL`
- `roleLabel: unknown = computed(() => { const held = new Set(this.auth.realmRoles().map((role) => role.toLowerCase())); const role = KNOWN_ROLES.find((candidate) => held.has(candidate…` — The role to show next to the name. One badge, not a list: a demo user holds one meaningful role, and a row of chips would suggest a permission model the application does not have. The highest-privilege match wins so that a Schichtleiter who also carries operator is not labelled the lesser of the two.
- `settingsOpen: unknown = signal(false)`
- `signOutOpen: unknown = signal(false)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `username: unknown = this.auth.username`

Methods:
- `confirmSignOut(): void` — Signs out, once the user has said so twice. The confirmation exists for the touchscreen. "Abmelden" sits in a header toolbar next to the language switch on a device operated with work gloves, and an accidental sign-out costs a full Keycloak round trip in the middle of a fault — the one moment nobody has time for it.
- `use(language: UiLanguage): void`

### ApprovalStateBadge

File: `src/app/shared/approval/approval-state.ts`
Selector: `app-approval-state`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: Whether a protocol has been vouched for, said in one place so it is said the same way everywhere. Why this is a component and not three copies of a span. Decision 1 of 2026-08-11 makes an unapproved protocol searchable and citable, and accepts the cost — it is less reliable to troubleshoot from. What makes that trade honest is that the state is never hidden: it appears on a source card under an answer, on a row in the Verwaltung table and in the viewer dialog. Three hand-written markers would eventually disagree about the wording, and the one that quietly dropped the "not approved" case is the one that turns the decision into a defect. Colour is never the only signal. Each state carries an icon AND a word, in both palettes, which is the same rule the footer health dot and the two answer modes follow. A reader with a colour vision deficiency, or one glancing at a tablet in plant lighting, gets the same information as everyone else. Approved is deliberately quiet, unapproved is deliberately not. Most of the corpus is approved, so a loud green badge on every row would be noise the eye learns to skip — and the moment it does, the marker that matters stops being noticed too. IT SAYS THE STATE AND NOTHING ELSE (2026-08-14). It used to name the approver and the day behind a {@code showActor} flag, and the flag is deleted rather than defaulted off: the longest form of it — "Freigegeben system:corpus-seed · 12.08.2026" — truncated in the Verwaltung table in production and ran under the action buttons. Who and when are PROVENANCE, and provenance belongs in the record rather than repeated in every list that mentions it. It is in the protocol viewer's history section now. The {@code language} input went with it: with no date to format, a required input that every one of four call sites had to supply was a cost with no purchase.

Inputs:
- `approval: Approval`

Properties:
- `approved: unknown = computed(() => this.approval().state === 'APPROVED')`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

### Dialog

File: `src/app/shared/dialog/dialog.ts`
Selector: `app-dialog`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The modal shell every dialog in this application is built from: backdrop, head with a title and a close button, scrolling body, focus trap, Esc. Why not \<dialog\> . The native element gives focus trapping and Esc for free, and it is the right choice in a browser — but the test runner is vitest in jsdom, which does not implement showModal() , so a native dialog would be untestable in the only place this project runs tests. The behaviour is therefore implemented here: Esc closes, Tab cycles inside, the first control takes focus on open and the opener gets it back on close. That is the part users notice; the element is an implementation detail. It was the help dialog's own code until the shop floor needed two more dialogs. Extracting it is what keeps "focus returns to the trigger" a property of every dialog rather than of the one that happened to be written first.

Inputs:
- `open: boolean = false`
- `testId: string = 'dialog'` — What the dialog is called in the DOM, so a test can address one dialog rather than "the dialog". The three parts get \<testId\>-backdrop , \<testId\>-dialog and \<testId\>-close .
- `title: string = ''`

Outputs:
- `closed: void`

Properties:
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `opener: HTMLElement | null = null` — Whoever opened the dialog, so focus can be handed back where it came from.
- `panel: unknown = viewChild<ElementRef<HTMLElement>>('panel')`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `` titleId: unknown = `dialog-title-${++sequence}` ``

Methods:
- `close(): void`
- `focusables(): HTMLElement[]` — The controls a user can actually reach inside the panel, in tab order. TWO EXCLUSIONS, AND BOTH ARE THERE BECAUSE THEIR ABSENCE BROKE SOMETHING. \`:not(\[disabled\])\` — a disabled control cannot take focus, and asking it to is a no-op that reports no error. When such a control happened to be first in the panel (the viewer's Download button, disabled until the document loads) the dialog opened with focus still on the page behind it, and Esc and the tab trap both stopped working, because both are bound to the backdrop and neither can see a key pressed outside it. \`:not(\[tabindex="-1"\])\` — \`\[tabindex\]\` on its own also matches the panel itself, which carries \`tabindex="-1"\` precisely so it can receive focus WITHOUT joining the tab ring. Without this exclusion the panel would become the first stop of a Tab cycle it is only the container of.
- `onKeydown(event: KeyboardEvent): void` — Esc closes from anywhere inside the dialog — the shortcut every modal is expected to have.
- `trapTab(event: KeyboardEvent): void` — Keeps Tab inside the dialog. Without this, tabbing walks out of a modal and onto the page behind it, which for a screen reader user means the dialog silently stops being where they are.

### HealthDot

File: `src/app/shared/health/health-dot.ts`
Selector: `app-health-dot`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The server-status dot in the footer. A component rather than a service, and the reason is its lifetime. The footer renders it only while someone is signed in, so "start polling on login" and "stop polling on logout" are just the component being created and destroyed — no second subscription to the auth signal, no token check duplicated from AuthService, and nothing left running behind a logged-out landing page. A service would have had to reproduce that lifecycle by hand and get it right twice. It is a glance surface, not a monitoring system. One failed request flips it to down. There is deliberately no hysteresis, no retry with backoff and no reconnect banner: a footer dot that stayed green through a real outage because it was waiting for a second opinion would be worse than no dot, and one that grew a state machine would be a monitoring feature nobody asked for. See the PR for the flapping question. Never colour alone. The dot is always beside its own text, because a status carried only by hue is a status some readers do not get — the same rule the answer modes follow (NFR-2).

Properties:
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `label: unknown = computed(() => { const labels = this.t().footer; switch (this.state()) { case 'up': return labels.serverUp; case 'down': return labels.serverDown; default: retu…`
- `state: unknown = signal<HealthState>('unknown')`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

Methods:
- `check(): void`

### Landing

File: `src/app/features/landing/landing.ts`
Selector: `app-landing`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The logged-out landing page: what this is, why it exists, and how to try it. It is the first screen a recruiter sees and it has about ninety seconds. So it leads with the problem rather than the stack, states the two things that make the answers trustworthy (sourced or labelled, processed in the EU), and puts the demo accounts and three questions that actually retrieve something within reach — a demo whose visitor cannot think of a question shows nothing. It replaces the Phase 1 login page and keeps its route, because postLogoutRedirectUri points at /login : signing out lands here, which is the right place to land.

Properties:
- `auth: unknown = inject(AuthService)`
- `demoBox: unknown = viewChild<ElementRef<HTMLElement>>('demoBox')`
- `demoPassword: unknown = DEMO_PASSWORD`
- `demoUsers: unknown = DEMO_USERS`
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `router: unknown = inject(Router)`
- `signedOut: unknown = signal(false)` — Set when this tab arrived here from a sign-out, so the landing page can confirm it happened.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

Methods:
- `jumpToDemo(): void` — Takes the visitor to the demo accounts further down the page. Focus moves with the scroll, not only the viewport. A scroll that leaves the keyboard where it was sends the next Tab back to the top of the page, and a screen reader never learns that anything happened — the button would work for a mouse and silently fail for everyone else. The target carries tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus without joining the tab order. Smooth unless the operating system asked for less motion, in which case it jumps: a full-page scroll is exactly the kind of movement that setting exists to stop.
- `signIn(username?: string): void` — Starts the redirect to Keycloak on an explicit click rather than on load: an automatic redirect turns any transient Keycloak error into a loop the visitor cannot escape. With a username it is the same redirect carrying login\_hint , so Keycloak prefills the field and the visitor only types the password. It is emphatically not a one-click login: see DECISIONS.txt on why the password grant and a credential-filling login theme were both rejected.

### Moderation

File: `src/app/features/moderation/moderation.ts`
Selector: `app-moderation`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The administrator's view of the corpus: everything that is in it, and the power to remove any of it. The admin role has had no shop-floor function until now — it administered Keycloak and saw an empty application. This is its function, and ADR-006 is why it exists: the write path is restricted for quality, which bounds volume and profanity but not a \*plausible\* protocol with a wrong Massnahme, filed by someone entitled to file it. Mode A cites that faithfully. Two things changed with ADR-006's 2026-08-10 revision. A protocol can be corrected in place — the old rule against it assumed stored answers, and this system generates every answer per query — and a deletion no longer destroys the protocol, it archives it. Both require a stated reason, and neither can be undone: there is no restore, and the edit dialog will not let anyone move a protocol to another machine, because machine identity is provenance rather than content. v1.2 splits the jobs. Approval is the administrator's, correction is the Schichtleiter's, and nobody holds both — so the row's buttons now depend on the reader's role rather than on the view they are standing in. See canCorrect and canApprove for what that means here and for the routing question it exposes. Duplicate detection, 2026-08-14, and the one rule it follows: it WARNS, it never blocks. Approving now asks first whether this machine already holds a protocol saying close to the same thing, and shows up to three if it does — with their dates, their similarity and, decisively, their OWN approval state. Nothing on this screen can refuse an approval on that basis, the approve button in the dialog is never disabled, and a failed similarity call approves anyway (approve). Four legitimate E-47 protocols on PR-03 describe four different root causes behind one fault code, and a feature that could turn "similar" into "refused" would have removed exactly the knowledge that makes the demo answer good.

Properties:
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `applied: unknown = signal<ProtocolFilter>(NO_FILTER)` — What the list on screen is actually narrowed to.
- `approvalFailure: unknown = signal<{ id: string; reason: ApiFailure } | null>(null)` — Why an approval was refused, and for which protocol. Held per row rather than as one page-level error: the reader clicked one button among ten, and a sentence at the top of the page about "this protocol" names none of them.
- `approvalNotice: unknown = signal<{ title: string; approved: boolean } | null>(null)` — What was just approved or un-approved, so the notice can name it.
- `approving: unknown = signal<string | null>(null)` — The protocol whose approval is being changed, while the request is in flight.
- `archiveCap: unknown = signal(0)`
- `archived: unknown = signal<readonly ArchivedProtocol[]>([])` — The archive, which is its own list with its own paging.
- `archiveLoading: unknown = signal(false)`
- `archiveMachine: unknown = signal('')`
- `archivePage: unknown = signal(0)`
- `archivePageCount: unknown = computed(() => Math.max(1, Math.ceil(this.archiveTotal() / PAGE_SIZE)), )`
- `archiveTotal: unknown = signal(0)`
- `auth: unknown = inject(AuthService)`
- `canApprove: unknown = computed(() => this.auth.realmRoles().includes('admin'))` — Who may approve. Admin only, here and — decisively — on the endpoint.
- `canArchive: unknown = this.canApprove` — Who may remove a protocol from the corpus, and read the archive of what was removed. The administrator, and nobody else — unchanged by 2026-08-14's widening. That change opened the corpus LIST and the DOCUMENT read to the Schichtleiter so their one write would be reachable; it opened nothing else, and this signal is where the interface says so. Absent rather than disabled. A Löschen button that exists only to refuse is noise on a shop-floor tablet, and worse, it tells the reader their role includes a power it does not.
- `canCorrect: unknown = computed(() => this.auth.realmRoles().includes('schichtleiter'))` — Who may CORRECT a protocol: the Schichtleiter, and since 2026-08-13 nobody else. The administrator lost this button, deliberately. Carlos's decision after reviewing #53: Techniker writes, Schichtleiter corrects, Admin approves, and nobody does two jobs. The backend refuses an admin's \`PUT\` with a 403, so leaving the button on screen would offer an action that cannot succeed — and a button that 403s is worse than an absent one, because the reader concludes the system is broken rather than that the job is not theirs. A FINDING TRAVELS WITH THIS, and it is not fixed here. \`/moderation\` is guarded by \`roleGuard('admin')\`, so a Schichtleiter cannot reach this view at all — which means the correction path now has no interface, for anyone. Widening the route is a permission decision that belongs to Carlos, not to this pull request, so the rule is written correctly here and the gap is reported. The day the route opens, this button is already right.
- `canDelete: unknown = computed(() => this.deleteComment().trim() !== '')`
- `canSaveEdit: unknown = computed( () => this.editTitle().trim() !== '' && this.editContent().trim() !== '' && this.editComment().trim() !== '', )` — Whether the correction can be submitted. The same three rules the backend enforces, checked here so the reader is told before the round trip rather than by a 400 afterwards. The backend keeps them regardless — a rule that exists only in the browser is a suggestion.
- `canWithdraw: unknown = computed(() => this.withdrawComment().trim() !== '')` — The backend refuses a withdrawal without a reason; so does this, before the round trip.
- `checkingDuplicates: unknown = signal<string | null>(null)` — Which protocol's similarity check is in flight, so its button can say it is working.
- `corrected: unknown = signal<string | null>(null)` — What was just corrected, so the notice can say it is being re-indexed.
- `deleteComment: unknown = signal('')` — Why it is being deleted. Required, here as well as on the server.
- `deleting: unknown = signal<ModeratedProtocol | null>(null)` — The protocol whose deletion is being confirmed, or null.
- `draft: unknown = signal<ProtocolFilter>(NO_FILTER)` — What the form currently holds — edited freely, and not yet asked for.
- `duplicates: unknown = signal<SimilarityReport | null>(null)` — What the check found. Null means no dialog — there is nothing to compare.
- `duplicatesBeyondShown: unknown = computed(() => { const report = this.duplicates(); return report ? report.total - report.candidates.length : 0; })` — How many cleared the threshold beyond the three shown. Zero renders nothing.
- `duplicatesOf: unknown = signal<ModeratedProtocol | null>(null)` — The protocol about to be approved, held while its similar siblings are on screen.
- `duplicatesOpen: unknown = computed( () => this.duplicates() !== null && this.viewingCandidate() === null, )` — Whether the duplicate list is on screen. It steps aside while a candidate is open in the viewer instead of stacking two modals: two focus traps in one page fight over Tab and Escape, and the alternative — closing this dialog to open the viewer — would throw away the list the reviewer is in the middle of comparing. Closing the viewer brings it straight back, with its state intact.
- `duplicateThresholdPercent: unknown = computed(() => Math.round((this.duplicates()?.threshold ?? 0) * 100), )` — The threshold as a whole percentage, for the one sentence that explains the numbers.
- `editComment: unknown = signal('')`
- `editContent: unknown = signal('')`

"Protokollverwaltung" describes reviewing and removing. A Schichtleiter does neither: they correct. Two roles behind one route need two names, or the wording quietly contradicts the buttons — which is the same defect as a control that only refuses, arriving through the door of the page title.
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `intro: unknown = computed(() => this.canApprove() ? this.t().moderation.intro : this.t().moderation.introCorrector, )`

- `language: unknown = this.i18n.language` — Passed to the date pipe, which cannot see a signal it is not given.
- `loading: unknown = signal(false)`
- `machineChosen: unknown = computed(() => this.draft().machineNo !== '')` — Whether the title and date fields are usable. The owner's rule, and the backend's: the machine comes first. Across ten machines a title fragment on its own answers with rows from machines the reviewer was not looking at. Disabling the fields says so before the request rather than after it — the 400 stays as a backstop for a caller that is not this form.
- `machines: unknown = signal<Machine[]>([])` — The machine dropdown's options. Readable by an admin since the ADR-006 role gained a job.
- `machinesFailed: unknown = signal(false)`

- `pageSize: unknown = PAGE_SIZE`

- `total: unknown = signal(0)`

- `viewingArchived: unknown = signal<ArchivedProtocol | null>(null)` — The archived protocol open in the viewer, or null — a different endpoint, so a different slot.
- `viewingCandidate: unknown = signal<SimilarProtocol | null>(null)` — A candidate open in the read-only viewer, or null.

- `withdrawing: unknown = signal<ModeratedProtocol | null>(null)` — The protocol whose approval is being withdrawn, or null. Withdrawal needs a reason.

Methods:
- `applyFilter(): void` — Applies the form. Back to page 0: page 3 of the old result is not page 3 of the new one.
- `approvalFailureFor(protocol: ModeratedProtocol): ApiFailure | null` — The refusal for THIS row, or null — so a sentence never appears beside the wrong protocol.
- `approve(protocol: ModeratedProtocol): void` — Starts an approval by asking what the corpus already says. The dialog appears only when there is something to look at. If nothing on this machine is similar, this is still the #54 behaviour — one click, no confirmation, because approving affirms text the reader has just read. A dialog that opened every time to announce "nothing found" would tax the common case to serve the rare one, and a permanently empty section is how a reader learns to click straight past a section that will one day be full. It fails OPEN, deliberately. A failed similarity call approves anyway rather than stopping the reviewer, and nothing is lost by it: the backend recomputes the same comparison inside the approval and writes what it found into the ledger, so the audit record is correct whether or not this call succeeded. The check here is an aid to a decision; it is not the decision, and it is not the record. Blocking an approval on a failed \*warning\* would invert the governing rule of the whole feature.
- `approveFromDialog(): void` — Approves the protocol whose similar siblings the reviewer has just been shown.
- `beginWithdraw(protocol: ModeratedProtocol): void` — Opens the withdrawal dialog on a protocol, carrying a reason over only when it belongs there. Both entry points go through here — the row button and the viewer — and neither may set \`withdrawing\` directly again. That is the whole fix: the reason is component state, so a dialog opened by assignment inherits whatever the last attempt left behind. THE TWO HALVES ARE SEPARABLE, and only one of them was ever wanted. RETRYING THE SAME PROTOCOL KEEPS THE SENTENCE: a network blip must not cost a reviewer the paragraph they just wrote, and asking them to type it again is how a withdrawal ends up with a thinner reason than the one it deserved. OPENING ANOTHER PROTOCOL STARTS BLANK: the reason is written into the moderation ledger and attributed as if meant about that protocol, so a sentence left in the box is one click from being permanently attached to a protocol nobody wrote it about. Convenience on one side, an unfixable record on the other. \`approvalFailure\` is the evidence of which protocol the retained reason belongs to — it already carries the failed target's id, for the refusal shown beside that row. A second signal tracking the same fact could disagree with it, and the two would then be right about different protocols.
- `cancelDelete(): void`
- `cancelEdit(): void`
- `cancelWithdraw(): void`
- `closeDuplicates(): void`
- `commitApproval(protocol: ModeratedProtocol): void` — Performs the approval itself. A failure is still reported beside the row it belongs to rather than at the top of the page, because the reader pressed one button among ten identical ones. What can fail is now narrower: the protocol was archived or removed by somebody else while this screen was open. The four-eyes refusal that used to be handled here is gone with the runtime check behind it (2026-08-15) — the property is carried by the role split and guarded by a test, and no response this client can receive says \`FOUR\_EYES\_REQUIRED\` any more.
- `confirmDelete(): void` — Removes the protocol whose deletion was confirmed. The list is reloaded rather than spliced: a delete changes the total, and therefore which rows belong on this page. Removing the row locally would leave a page of nine and a pagination footer quietly describing a corpus that no longer exists.
- `confirmWithdraw(): void` — Withdraws approval, with the reason the backend requires and the reader is owed.
- `edit(field: string | number | symbol, value: string): void` — Edits one field of the form.
- `filterArchive(machineNo: string): void`
- `filterByApproval(state: ProtocolFilter): void` — Applies the approval filter immediately, without the Filter button. It is not part of the machine-first form: it needs no machine, it has one value, and a queue a reviewer has to press a second control to see is a queue they will stop opening. The other four fields keep the button, because they are a form that is filled in and then submitted.
- `load(page: number): void`
- `loadArchive(page: number): void`
- `next(): void`
- `nextArchive(): void`
- `openCandidate(candidate: SimilarProtocol): void` — Opens one candidate in the read-only viewer. The duplicate dialog steps aside rather than stacking a second modal on top of itself — see duplicatesOpen. Two focus traps in one page is a bug looking for a keyboard, and closing this one would lose the list the reviewer is halfway through comparing. It comes back when the viewer does.
- `percent(similarity: number): number` — A cosine similarity as a whole percentage. Rounded to no decimals deliberately: 93.05 % beside 92.87 % invites a reviewer to treat the difference as meaningful, and it is not — the decision this number informs is "open both and read them", which 93 % and 93 % answer identically.
- `previous(): void`
- `previousArchive(): void`
- `resetFilter(): void` — Clears the form and the list back to the whole corpus.
- `saveEdit(): void` — Submits the correction. Machine and type are sent back exactly as they arrived. The dialog shows them read-only and the backend refuses a change, so this is an echo rather than an input — but it is sent, because a request that omitted them would be a request that could be built by a client that thought they were optional.
- `showTab(tab: "corpus" | "archive"): void`
- `startEdit(protocol: ModeratedProtocol): void` — Opens the edit dialog and fetches the text to correct. The current document is loaded rather than reconstructed from the row: title and errorCode live on the protocol, but the thing being corrected is the document on the volume, and an edit form pre-filled with anything else would silently replace the text with whatever the form happened to know.
- `statusLabel(status: ModeratedProtocol): string`

### Pager

File: `src/app/shared/pager/pager.ts`
Selector: `app-pager`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The paging control the three tables share: a labelled arrow either side of "page X of Y". The buttons carry their text, not only a chevron. The primary device is a shop-floor tablet operated with work gloves, and a bare arrow is both a smaller target and a guess — "Zurück" next to a table could as easily mean leaving the view. Spelling out "Vorherige Seite" / "Nächste Seite" costs width the page has and removes the guess. Extracted rather than copied into each table because there are three of them now (the corpus, the archive and "Meine Uploads") and the disabled-at-the-ends rule is the kind of thing that gets fixed in one of three places. Zero-based page in, one-based on screen: the API pages from 0 and people count from 1, and the conversion belongs in one place rather than at every call site.

Inputs:
- `label: string = ''` — What the pager is called for a screen reader, when a view has more than one.
- `page: number` — Zero-based, as the API counts.
- `pageCount: number`
- `testId: string = 'pager'` — Suffix for the test ids, so two pagers on one screen are addressable apart.
- `total: number` — Rows in the whole result, so the control can say what it is paging through.

Outputs:
- `next: void`
- `previous: void`

Properties:
- `hasNext: unknown = computed(() => this.page() + 1 < this.pageCount())`
- `hasPrevious: unknown = computed(() => this.page() > 0)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

### ProtocolDialog

File: `src/app/shared/protocol/protocol-dialog.ts`
Selector: `app-protocol-dialog`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The in-app protocol viewer. Why the document no longer leaves the application. #26 fetched the protocol as a blob through HttpClient — necessary, because a browser-followed anchor carries no Bearer token — and then opened it in a new tab as an object URL. That solved the 401 and left the reader in the browser's raw text viewer: unstyled, outside the application, and on a shop-floor tablet or a kiosk terminal a place that is genuinely hard to get back from. Rendering it here removes the category of problem instead of working around it: nothing navigates, so nothing can navigate without a token, and the synchronous window.open dance with its popup-blocker fallback is simply gone. The request itself is unchanged — the same GET /api/protocols/{id}/document through the same interceptor. The backend was not touched. The download action is the one remaining use of a blob URL in the application, and it is the right one: saving a file is exactly what an object URL is for.

Inputs:
- `approval: Approval | null = null` — The protocol's approval, when the caller knows it. Null renders nothing. Optional because the three callers differ in what they hold: the Verwaltung row carries a full Approval, a citation carries only a boolean widened into one, and the archive carries none — approving something withdrawn from the corpus means nothing, and the backend refuses it.
- `machine: string = ''` — The machine the question was asked about — the second half of "which document is this".
- `protocolId: string | null = null` — The protocol to show, or null when the viewer is closed. Setting it starts the fetch.
- `protocolTitle: string = ''` — What the answer called this protocol, so the dialog names what the reader clicked.
- `source: DocumentSource = 'citation'` — Which endpoint to read the document from. The same file, fetched over a path with a different authorisation rule: citation is the shop-floor path, open to the three roles that ask questions, and moderation is the admin one. An admin holds no shop-floor role, so a viewer hard-wired to the first would 403 for exactly the person this dialog was reused for.

Outputs:
- `closed: void`

Properties:
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `canDownload: unknown = computed(() => this.file() !== null)` — Whether a download is possible — the bytes are here even when parsing gave up on them.
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `events: unknown = computed(() => this.history()?.events ?? [])` — The events to render, or an empty list. Already capped by the backend to ProtocolHistory.limit; this does not slice again. Two places enforcing one cap is two places for it to drift, and the server's is the one that bounds the payload.
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `file: unknown = signal<{ blob: Blob; filename: string } | null>(null)` — Held so the download saves the ORIGINAL bytes, not a re-encoding of the parsed text.
- `hasHistorySection: unknown = computed( () => this.events().length > 0 || this.showsApprovalProvenance(), )` — Nothing to say: no events, and no approval to attribute. An empty box would be worse.
- `history: unknown = signal<ProtocolHistory | null>(null)` — What has been done to this protocol, or null when it was not asked for. Only fetched on the moderation paths. \`citation\` is the shop floor's viewer, and the endpoint answers 403 for those roles by design — who corrected what and who took an approval back names colleagues in connection with mistakes, which is moderation information. A technician checking a citation gets the text and the approval STATE, both of which they already have.
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `language: unknown = this.i18n.language` — Handed down to the date pipe inside the badge, which is pure and cannot read a signal.
- `loading: unknown = signal(false)`
- `objectUrl: string | null = null`
- `olderEvents: unknown = computed(() => { const history = this.history(); return history ? history.total - history.events.length : 0; })` — How many acts exist beyond the ones shown. THE CAP IS A PRODUCT DECISION, NOT A TECHNICAL LIMIT (see \`ProtocolModerationService\`): the viewer exists to let somebody read a protocol, and three lines answer "what happened to this recently" without pushing the document below the fold. A full change history is a REPORT with its own screen, deferred deliberately. This number is what stops the truncation being silent — it is not an invitation to add a "show all" control here.
- `parsed: unknown = signal<ProtocolDocument | null>(null)`
- `showsApprovalProvenance: unknown = computed( () => this.wantsHistory() && this.events().length === 0 && (this.approval()?.approvedBy ?? null) !== null, )` — Whether to fall back to the approval columns instead of a ledger. The seeded case, and it is a true statement rather than a placeholder. The 150 protocols the corpus was built from were approved by the V5 migration itself — \`system:corpus-seed\`, no human act — so they have no ledger rows and never will. Showing nothing at all would imply the approval came from somewhere it did not; showing the actor once, here, is the honest record of the decision that seeded them.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `wantsHistory: unknown = computed(() => this.source() !== 'citation')` — Whether the reader may see a history at all. The same rule the endpoint enforces.

Methods:
- `actionLabel(action: ModerationEvent): string` — The verb for one ledger action, so UNAPPROVE never reaches a screen.
- `close(): void`
- `download(): void` — Saves the original file. An object URL rather than a link to the API for the same reason the viewer exists: a download the browser performs from an /api/ href is a fresh navigation with no token on it.
- `load(protocolId: string): void`
- `loadHistory(protocolId: string): void` — Fetches the ledger, and fails silently when it cannot. A failure here leaves the history absent rather than putting an error in the dialog. The viewer's job is to show a protocol; the history is context beside it, and a red box about an unreachable audit trail would sit next to a document that loaded perfectly and read as though the document were the problem. The document's own failure has a message, because that one is the dialog failing at what it is for. Note the fallback below still runs: a protocol whose history call failed but whose approval columns are present shows the provenance line, which is true whatever happened to this request.
- `ngOnDestroy(): void`
- `releaseObjectUrl(): void` — An object URL pins its blob in memory until it is revoked, so a technician clicking through six sources would otherwise leave six documents allocated for the life of the tab. At most one download is live at a time, so holding exactly one and releasing it on the next is enough — and it is not released on close, because a download the user started a moment ago may still be reading it.
- `reset(): void`

### Search

File: `src/app/features/search/search.ts`
Selector: `app-search`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The search view (US-1/US-2): the question form, and the two things that answer it. Two columns on a wide screen — the form and its answer on the left, the help panel on the right — and one column below 64rem. The answer belongs directly under the form that produced it: it rendered after the help panel before, which meant scrolling past an explanation to reach the thing being explained. The answer block itself is SearchAnswer. The two modes are visually distinct there, which is not styling but NFR-2: a Mode B answer that looked like a Mode A one would be the failure this application exists to prevent.

Properties:
- `answer: unknown = signal<QueryAnswer | null>(null)`
- `answeredApprovedOnly: unknown = signal(false)` — What the answer on screen was actually asked with — see SearchAnswer.approvedOnly.
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `approvedOnly: unknown = signal(false)` — The approved-only facet, OFF by default. The default is decision 1 of 2026-08-11, not a convenience: an unapproved protocol stays searchable because the administrator may not review at a weekend and the factory does not stop. Defaulting this ON would quietly reinstate the gate that decision refused, and would do it in the one place nobody would look for it.
- `asking: unknown = signal(false)`
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `machineId: unknown = signal('')`
- ``machineLabel: unknown = computed(() => { const machine = this.machines().find((candidate) => candidate.id === this.machineId()); return machine ? `${machine.machineNo} · ${machine.name…`` — What to call the machine in the viewer's head: the picker's own label, not an id.
- `machines: unknown = signal<Machine[]>([])`
- `machinesFailed: unknown = signal(false)`
- `question: unknown = signal('')`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `validation: unknown = signal<'question' | 'machine' | null>(null)`
- `viewing: unknown = signal<Citation | null>(null)` — The citation whose protocol the viewer is showing, or null when the viewer is closed.
- `viewingApproval: unknown = computed<Approval | null>(() => { const citation = this.viewing(); return citation ? { state: citation.approved ? 'APPROVED' : 'UNAPPROVED', approvedBy: null, a…` — The open source's approval, for the viewer's head, or null when nothing is open. The state travels into the dialog rather than being looked up there, so the mark a reader saw on the source card is the same mark they see on the document — one fact, told once. A second fetch could also disagree with the card if an administrator approved it in the meantime, and a source list that contradicts the document it links to is worse than a slightly stale one.

Methods:
- `ask(): void`
- `openSource(citation: Citation, event?: Event): void` — Opens the protocol behind a citation, in a dialog, inside the application. Why this is a handler and not an href . It was an href , and it did not work: a browser-followed anchor is a fresh navigation that never passes through Angular's interceptor chain, so it carries no Authorization header, and the backend is a stateless JWT resource server with no cookie fallback — every click answered 401. The first fix (#26) fetched the document through HttpClient and opened it in a new tab as an object URL. That was right about the token and wrong about the destination: it dropped the reader into the browser's raw text viewer, out of the application, which on a shop-floor tablet is somewhere hard to come back from. The viewer dialog keeps the document here, and the whole question of what a navigation carries stops applying. All this method does now is name the citation — the dialog owns the fetch, the parsing and the download.
- `widenToWholeCorpus(): void` — Turns the facet off and asks the same question again. Offered from the Mode B note, because that is the moment the narrowing is felt: the reader has an unsourced answer and no way of telling whether the corpus is empty on this fault or merely unreviewed. Re-asking rather than merely unchecking, so the answer follows the decision.

### SearchAnswer

File: `src/app/features/search/search-answer.ts`
Selector: `app-search-answer`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The answer block: the two modes, the citation markers, and the source list under them. Its own component for two reasons. It is where the clamp below has to live — the drawer and the citation markers must be able to talk to each other without the search view brokering it — and the search view was otherwise carrying the markup and the stylesheet for something that is not about asking a question. The clamp is visual and nothing else. The full answer is in the DOM at all times: it is never truncated, never paginated and never split. A Mode A answer's claims each name the source they came from, and cutting the text would separate a claim from its citation — the exact guarantee NFR-2 rests on. \`max-height\` and \`overflow: hidden\` are the whole mechanism, so expanding reveals text that was already there rather than fetching or rebuilding anything.

Inputs:
- `answer: QueryAnswer`
- `approvedOnly: boolean = false` — Whether THIS answer was produced with the approved-only facet on. The state of the answer, not of the checkbox: a reader who toggles the facet after asking has not changed what they are looking at, and a note that flipped with the control would describe a search that was never run.
- `machine: string = ''` — What to call the machine on a source card read on its own.

Outputs:
- `opened: Citation` — A source's title was activated — the search view owns the viewer dialog.
- `widen: void` — The reader asked to search the whole corpus after all — the search view re-runs the query.

Properties:
- `body: unknown = viewChild<ElementRef<HTMLElement>>('answerBody')`
- `clamped: unknown = computed(() => this.overflowing() && !this.expanded())`
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `expanded: unknown = signal(false)`
- `focusedSource: unknown = signal<SourceFocus | null>(null)` — The source a citation marker last pointed at; handed to the list, which reveals it.
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `overflowing: unknown = signal(false)` — Whether the answer is long enough to be worth a drawer. Measured, not guessed.
- `segments: unknown = computed<AnswerSegment[]>(() => { const current = this.answer(); return current.mode === 'A' ? toSegments(current.answer, current.citations) : []; })`
- `steps: unknown = computed<string[]>(() => { const current = this.answer(); if (current.mode !== 'B') { return []; } return current.answer .split('\n') .map((step) => step.trim()…` — Mode B's steps: the backend joins them with newlines, and they render as a numbered list.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `unapprovedCount: unknown = computed( () => this.answer().citations.filter((citation) => !citation.approved).length, )` — How many of the cited sources nobody has approved. Said ONCE at the answer level, in addition to the per-source markers below, and both are needed. Decision 1 of 2026-08-11 keeps unapproved protocols searchable and accepts that they are less reliable to troubleshoot from — the price of that trade is that the reader is told. A technician who has to read down a list of five source cards to discover that one of them is unreviewed has effectively not been told: the answer is what they act on, and on a tablet the sources may not even be on screen. Zero when every source is approved, which is the ordinary case and renders nothing at all.

Methods:
- `limitPx(): number` — Half the viewport, from the same window the element is rendered in.
- `measure(): void` — Decides whether the drawer is needed, by measuring the rendered answer. Measured rather than counted in characters: how tall an answer is depends on the viewport, the text scale the reader chose (the design system is rem-based, so "large" genuinely means taller) and where the lines break. A character threshold would clamp a short answer on a phone and miss a long one on a desktop.
- `showSource(citation: Citation): void` — Follows a \[P1\] marker to the card it names. Expands first, then points. A marker that scrolled to a source while the answer above it was still clamped — or worse, did nothing visible because the clamp swallowed the movement — is the #26 bug class returning in a new costume: a citation control that answers a click with nothing. Opening the drawer is therefore part of following the marker, not a separate step the reader has to think of. A fresh object every time, because a signal set to the value it already holds notifies nobody and the second click on the same marker has to work as well as the first.
- `similarityPercent(citation: Citation): number` — Percent, rounded — a reader compares 69 % with 56 %, not 0.6896 with 0.5566.
- `toggle(): void`

### SearchHelp

File: `src/app/features/search/search-help.ts`
Selector: `app-search-help`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: "Wie suche ich?" — the panel in the empty right half of the search view. It is the designed answer to the lazy-query problem, not decoration. A user who does not know how retrieval behaves types one word, gets Mode B, and concludes the assistant is broken. Explaining the rule beside the field costs a paragraph. THE PANEL TRACKS RETRIEVAL BEHAVIOUR, AND IT HAS BEEN WRONG ONCE. Until 2026-08-20 it taught that "ein Wort beschreibt keinen Fehler, und die Suche hat nichts, womit sie vergleichen kann". That was true while retrieval was semantic only (ADR-004) and was FALSIFIED BY THE RUNNING SYSTEM once ADR-009 added the lexical signal: a bare "E-47" now returns a grounded Mode A answer, because {@code LexicalTerms} matches codes literally. Carlos's v1.3.0 drill typed it and watched it work while this panel said it would not. The text now states the rule the code actually implements: a term needs at least one LETTER and at least one DIGIT to be matched literally. That is why "E-47" and "SV0410" work on their own while "frei", "Druck" and "Band" still do not — and it is why a change to {@code LexicalTerms} is also a change to this file. A help panel that contradicts observable behaviour is worse than none: it teaches the reader to distrust the one thing on screen meant to orient them. No validation gate , decided 2026-08-20 and not to be re-proposed. Refusing to search until a question "looks complete" would block "e-47" — a lazy query that WORKS — in order to prevent "was bedeutet", which Mode B already handles gracefully. The cure costs more than the disease. Its own component because the styling is a third of the search view's stylesheet and none of it is about answers. That also keeps \`search.css\` inside the per-component budget, which the combined file had just exceeded. Subordinate by construction : no card, no shadow, helper-grey text behind a left rule. Once an answer arrives it must not compete with it — the answer is what the reader came for.

Properties:
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `open: unknown = signal(false)` — Whether the panel is open. Only narrow viewports read this: on a wide screen the panel sits beside the form and the stylesheet keeps it open regardless, because collapsing something already next to the field it explains costs a click and buys nothing. Closed by default, so a phone shows the form first.
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`

### ThemeToggle

File: `src/app/shared/theme/theme-toggle.ts`

Description: The theme control: light and dark, with the operating system as the silent default. There is no "system" button. Until the user presses one of these two, the application follows prefers-color-scheme and says nothing about it — a first visit already does the right thing, and a third segment explaining that costs a third of the control to state the default. With no stored choice neither button would be pressed if it tracked the choice, and the control would look broken on a first visit. ### Upload

File: `src/app/features/upload/upload.ts`
Selector: `app-upload`
Standalone: yes
Change detection: `ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush`

Description: The Schichtleiter's upload view. Write access belongs to one role by decision (DECISIONS.txt: quality, consistency, anti-garbage), and the route is guarded accordingly — but the guard is convenience. The backend refuses the upload for anyone else, which is the check that counts (NFR-3). The view is built around the fact that upload answers 202, not 201 : the protocol exists but is not searchable until a worker has chunked and embedded it. Hiding that behind a success message would teach a Schichtleiter that uploading and being findable are the same event, and the first time indexing failed they would have no idea. So the status list is part of the view, and it shows the failure reason rather than only the failure. A protocol can be typed here as well as uploaded. Requiring a .txt described a workflow that does not exist: the Schichtleiter writes the protocol at the end of the shift, and nobody opens an editor, saves a file and then picks it. Typing is the normal case and the file was the special one. The typed text is wrapped into a File in the browser and sent through the same multipart call , which is why this is a frontend-only change: the endpoint, the ingestion pipeline, the volume, the citation path and the download all stay unaware, and a typed protocol is indistinguishable from an uploaded one the moment it is submitted. A backend "text" field would have been a second write path to keep in step with the first, for no gain the user can see.

Properties:
- `accepted: unknown = signal(false)`
- `api: unknown = inject(MaintenanceApiService)`
- `canSubmit: unknown = computed(() => { if (!this.machineNo() || !this.title().trim()) { return false; } return this.mode() === 'file' ? this.file() !== null : this.text().trim().leng…` — Whether there is something to submit. A machine, a title, and content in whichever mode is active. The title is required in both modes because a protocol without one cannot be reviewed in any list — "Meine Uploads" would show a machine number and a date, and the Schichtleiter would have to open each row to find out which one is which. Deliberately shallow beyond that: size caps and rate limits belong to the upload-guards work and are not smuggled in here — a validation rule that exists only in the browser is a suggestion, and the place to make it a rule is the backend.
- `errorCode: unknown = signal('')`
- `failure: unknown = signal<ApiFailure | null>(null)`
- `file: unknown = signal<File | null>(null)`
- `fileInput: unknown = viewChild<ElementRef<HTMLInputElement>>('fileInput')` — The native file input, so switching modes can actually clear it. Setting the file signal to null is not enough: the input keeps showing the chosen filename, and the form would be telling the user one thing while holding another.
- `i18n: unknown = inject(I18nService)`
- `language: unknown = this.i18n.language` — Passed to the date pipe, which cannot see a signal it is not given.
- `machineNo: unknown = signal('')`
- `machines: unknown = signal<Machine[]>([])`
- `mode: unknown = signal<InputMode>('file')`
- `page: unknown = signal(0)` — Zero-based page of "Meine Uploads".
- `pageCount: unknown = computed(() => Math.max(1, Math.ceil(this.uploads().length / PAGE_SIZE)), )`
- `pagedUploads: unknown = computed(() => { const start = this.page() * PAGE_SIZE; return this.uploads().slice(start, start + PAGE_SIZE); })` — The rows on screen. Paged in the browser, and that is a deliberate limit rather than the right answer. {@code GET /api/protocols/mine} returns the caller's 50 most recent uploads in one response and has no paging of its own; adding some would be a backend change, and this PR does not touch the backend. Fifty rows is small enough that slicing them here costs nothing and reads the same to the user. If that endpoint ever grows past its cap, this has to become a server-side page — client-side paging of a truncated list would quietly page through the wrong fifty.
- `refreshing: unknown = signal(false)`
- `submitting: unknown = signal(false)`
- `t: unknown = this.i18n.t`
- `text: unknown = signal('')`
- `title: unknown = signal('')`
- `type: unknown = signal<'STOERUNG' | 'WARTUNG'>('STOERUNG')`
- `uploads: unknown = signal<UploadStatus[]>([])`

Methods:
- `clearFileInput(): void`
- `isMode(mode: InputMode): boolean` — Which mode's panel to show — and, for the segmented control, which button is pressed.
- `nextPage(): void`
- `pickFile(event: Event): void`
- `previousPage(): void`
- `refresh(): void` — Reloads the status list on demand. Manual rather than polled. Indexing takes seconds, a poll would run for the whole time the tab is open, and every one of those requests costs a database round trip to answer "still the same". A button the user presses when they care is smaller, cheaper and easier to reason about than a timer somebody has to remember to clear.
- `statusLabel(status: UploadStatus): string`
- `submit(): void`
- `typedFile(): File` — The typed protocol, as the file the upload endpoint already knows how to take. text/plain and the trimmed text: the ingestion pipeline reads UTF-8 text off the volume and chunks it by paragraph, and that is exactly what this is. Nothing downstream can tell the difference, which is the whole design.
- `useMode(mode: InputMode): void` — Switches input mode and drops whatever the other mode was holding. Keeping it would mean a form that submits something the user cannot see — they typed a protocol, switched to file to check something, switched back, and a stale file is still attached. Cheaper to lose one input on an explicit mode switch than to submit a surprise.

## Pipes

### AppDatePipe

File: `src/app/core/i18n/app-date.pipe.ts`
Pipe name: `appDate`
Standalone: yes

Description: A date, in the format the interface language uses. Why the language is an argument rather than something the pipe reads. The obvious shape is to inject I18nService and read the signal inside \`transform\` — and it produces a pipe that goes stale. A pure pipe re-runs only when its \*inputs\* change, and switching language changes no input on a table cell, so half the screen would keep the old format until something else happened to redraw it. Passing \`language()\` makes the language an input, which is what Angular needs to know the answer changed. The alternative, \`pure: false\`, hides the same dependency behind a pipe that recomputes on every change-detection pass forever. It delegates to Angular's own DatePipe rather than to \`toLocaleDateString\`, which is what the two views did before: the browser's implementation answers to the \*browser's\* idea of a locale and quietly varies between engines, while this is the same formatter the rest of the framework uses and is pinned to registered locale data. Invalid or missing input returns what it was given rather than "Invalid Date". A row with a broken timestamp should still show the reviewer what is stored.

Methods:
- `transform(value: string | Date | null | undefined, language: UiLanguage, withTime: unknown = false): string` — Example : keeps the day-only format it was written for — the viewer's history is the one place that needs the minute, and a default that changed under twenty call sites would be a formatting change disguised as a feature.

## Services / Injectables

### AuthService

File: `src/app/core/auth/auth.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: Wraps angular-oauth2-oidc so components never touch the OIDC library directly. Roles are read from the access token , not the ID token: Keycloak puts realm roles in realm\_access.roles there. They drive what the UI shows — the backend enforces the same roles server-side, because hiding a button is not a security control (NFR-3).

Properties:
- `authState: unknown = signal(0)` — Bumped after every login/logout so the derived signals recompute.
- `configService: unknown = inject(ConfigService)`
- `isAuthenticated: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.oauth.hasValidAccessToken(); })`
- `oauth: unknown = inject(OAuthService)`
- `realmRoles: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.claims()?.realm_access?.roles ?? []; })`
- `signedInAt: unknown = computed<Date | null>(() => { this.authState(); const issuedAt = this.claims()?.iat; if (typeof issuedAt !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(issuedAt)) { return nu…` — When this session's token was issued, or null if the claim is missing or nonsensical. Null rather than a guess: "signed in since" is a fact or it is nothing, and a fabricated time on a settings screen is worse than an absent row. The token's iat is the honest answer to the question the user is asking — the session ends 15 minutes after it (ADR-005).
- `username: unknown = computed(() => { this.authState(); return this.claims()?.preferred_username ?? ''; })`

Methods:
- `claims(): AccessTokenClaims | null` — Decodes the access token payload; returns null when there is no valid token.
- `consumeSignedOutNotice(): boolean` — Whether this tab has just signed out, clearing the flag as it reports it. Read-and-clear rather than read: the notice is about the sign-out that just happened, and one that reappeared on every later visit to the landing page would stop meaning anything.
- `init(): Promise<void>` — Configures the client, fetches the discovery document and completes a redirect that is coming back from Keycloak. Runs once during application startup.
- `login(loginHint?: string): void` — Sends the browser to Keycloak's login page. loginHint is passed as the standard login\_hint authorization request parameter, which Keycloak uses to prefill the username field. It is a hint on the normal Auth Code + PKCE request and nothing more: the visitor still authenticates at Keycloak, and the password never passes through this application. The demo buttons on the landing page are its only caller.
- `logout(): void`
- `rememberSignOut(): void`

### ConfigService

File: `src/app/core/config/config.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: Loads RuntimeConfig from /config.json once, during startup. A missing or malformed file is not an error: the values compiled into environment.ts are used instead. That keeps the image runnable on its own — a deployment that forgets the bind mount serves the built-in defaults rather than a blank page.

Properties:
- `current: RuntimeConfig = this.fallback`
- `fallback: RuntimeConfig = { keycloakIssuer: environment.keycloakIssuer, keycloakClientId: environment.keycloakClientId, apiBaseUrl: environment.apiBaseUrl, }`

Methods:
- `load(): Promise<void>` — Fetched with fetch rather than HttpClient on purpose: this runs before the first route renders, and the interceptor chain HttpClient carries is set up to attach an access token that does not exist yet.

### FontScaleService

File: `src/app/core/theme/font-scale.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: Application-wide font scaling, in three steps. Why this is one attribute and not a stylesheet. The design system is rem-based throughout — every spacing step, every type size, every touch target — so moving the root font size moves the whole interface together, including the 44 px tap targets, which is the half that matters on a tablet. A second set of sizes would be a second design system to keep in step with the first. The audience is stated rather than assumed: this application is read on small machinery-mounted screens by technicians who are frequently not twenty-five. Browser zoom does the same job and is the wrong answer here — it is per-origin, it is buried in a menu on a kiosk browser, and on a locked-down shop-floor tablet the user often cannot reach it at all.

Properties:
- `current: unknown = signal<FontScale>(storedScale())`
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `scale: unknown = this.current.asReadonly()`

Methods:
- `apply(scale: FontScale): void`
- `use(scale: FontScale): void`

### I18nService

File: `src/app/core/i18n/i18n.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The DE/EN switch, as a runtime dictionary rather than Angular's build-time i18n. Angular's $localize produces one bundle per locale, which means two builds, two images and a routing or host decision to pick between them. For two languages and one small application that is a deployment problem bought to solve a string problem — and it would make the language a property of the URL rather than of the person, so switching would reload the page and lose the answer on screen. A signal holding one of two typed objects switches instantly and ships one bundle. The UI language is not the answer language. The backend pins every answer to the language of the question (ADR-002's language rule), and nothing is translated anywhere in this system by decision. So a German answer stays German with the interface in English: this service changes labels, never content. The rendered answer carries its own lang attribute for exactly that reason.

Properties:
- `current: unknown = signal<UiLanguage>(initialLanguage())`
- `language: unknown = this.current.asReadonly()` — The active language, for lang attributes and for the switch's own state.
- `t: unknown = computed<Dictionary>(() => DICTIONARIES[this.current()])` — The active dictionary. Components read t().search.submit and re-render on a switch.

Methods:
- `toggle(): void`
- `use(language: UiLanguage): void`

### MaintenanceApiService

File: `src/app/core/api/maintenance-api.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The handful of calls this application makes to its own backend. One service rather than one per feature: the API is small, and splitting it would mean three files that each inject the same base URL to make one request. The access token is attached by angular-oauth2-oidc 's resource-server interceptor, configured once in app.config.ts , so nothing here touches a header.

Properties:
- `apiBaseUrl: unknown = inject(ConfigService).config.apiBaseUrl`
- `http: unknown = inject(HttpClient)`

Methods:
- `ask(question: string, machineId: string, approvedOnly: unknown = false): Observable<QueryAnswer>` — Asks a question about one machine. Search is scoped to exactly one machine by decision, so machineId is required rather than optional-with-a-default: a question answered from another machine's protocols would look like a better feature and be a worse answer.
- `deletedProtocols(machineNo: string, page: number, size: number): Observable<DeletedProtocolPage>` — One page of the archive: what was removed, by whom and why. Admin only, server-side.
- `deleteProtocol(protocolId: string, comment: string): Observable<void>` — Removes a protocol from the corpus and moves it into the archive. Admin only, server-side. The comment travels in a body rather than a query string, matching the endpoint: a sentence about a named colleague's mistake would otherwise land in access logs, proxy logs and browser history — three places nobody audited for it.
- `editProtocol(protocolId: string, correction: ProtocolCorrection): Observable<UploadAccepted>` — Corrects a protocol in place. Answers 202: the text is fixed, the search index is not yet. Re-indexing is the backend's condition of the edit rather than a follow-up call from here — a correction that could be applied without one would leave retrieval matching text the document no longer contains (ADR-006 revision).
- `getArchivedDocument(protocolId: string): Observable<HttpResponse<Blob>>` — The document of an archived protocol. A third document call rather than a parameter on one, for the reason the second one exists: they differ in what they are allowed to serve. This is the only door back to a removed protocol's content, and it is what makes the archive evidence rather than a tombstone.
- `getDocument(protocolId: string): Observable<HttpResponse<Blob>>` — Fetches a protocol's original document. Through HttpClient, and that is the whole point. This used to be a method returning the URL for an \<a href\> , and it did not work: a browser-followed anchor is a fresh navigation that never passes through Angular's interceptor chain, so it carries no Authorization header. The backend is a stateless JWT resource server with no session and no cookie fallback ( SecurityConfig ), so every such click answered 401. Returning a URL at all is what invited the mistake, so no method here returns one. observe: 'response' rather than the body alone because the response headers are the useful half: Content-Type decides whether the browser renders the document or downloads it, and Content-Disposition carries the readable filename the backend built.
- `getModerationDocument(protocolId: string): Observable<HttpResponse<Blob>>` — A protocol's document through the moderation path. A separate call from getDocument rather than a parameter, because they differ in who may make them: the shop-floor path is open to the three roles that ask questions, and an admin holds none of them. Same file, same mechanics, different authorisation — which is exactly the kind of difference that should be visible at the call site.
- `health(): Observable<HealthStatus>` — Whether the backend is answering. Public server-side — no token is required — but the request still goes through the same HttpClient and therefore still carries the Bearer token the interceptor attaches. That is harmless on a public endpoint, and a bypass built to avoid it would be a second HTTP path to keep in step with the first for no gain.
- `machines(): Observable<Machine[]>` — The machines a question can be asked about.
- `moderationProtocols(page: number, size: number, filter: ProtocolFilter = NO_FILTER): Observable<ProtocolPage>` — One page of the whole corpus. Admin only, server-side. Paged rather than "give me everything": the corpus is 150 protocols and grows every time one is uploaded, and a review screen that loads all of them gets slower every month.
- `myUploads(): Observable<UploadStatus[]>` — The caller's own uploads and what became of them. Schichtleiter only, server-side.
- `protocolHistory(protocolId: string): Observable<ProtocolHistory>` — What has been done to one protocol, newest first. ADMIN and SCHICHTLEITER, server-side. Capped by the backend rather than here: a protocol edited weekly for a year has fifty rows, and fetching all of them so a dialog can drop forty-seven is a payload that grows with the corpus's age. The response carries total so the viewer can still say that older entries exist.
- `setApproval(protocolId: string, approved: boolean, comment: string = ''): Observable<Approval>` — Approves a protocol, or withdraws approval. Admin only, server-side. A state is asserted rather than a verb performed — PUT of {approved} rather than two endpoints — so a double-clicked button is harmless and writes no second audit row. The comment is REQUIRED to withdraw and optional to grant, and travels in the body for the same reason the delete comment does: it can name a colleague's mistake, and a query string lands in access logs, proxy logs and browser history.
- `similarProtocols(protocolId: string): Observable<SimilarityReport>` — Protocols on the same machine that say close to what this one says. Admin only, server-side. A read, and only ever a read. It is asked before an approval so the approver can compare, and the approval itself does not depend on it: the backend recomputes the same comparison and writes what it found into the ledger, so an approval made without ever calling this records the same fact. That is what makes it safe for the view to fail open when this call errors — see Moderation.approve .
- `upload(form: FormData): Observable<UploadAccepted>` — Uploads a protocol document. Answers 202: stored, not yet searchable.

### ThemeService

File: `src/app/core/theme/theme.service.ts`
providedIn: `root`

Description: The theme, as a three-state choice with the operating system as the default. Why the operating system is resolved here rather than by a media query. The dark palette used to live in @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) . A manual override on top of that needs the dark values to apply under two conditions at once — the media query and an attribute — and CSS has no way to share one declaration block between them, so the values would exist twice and drift apart the first time one of them was edited. Resolving the preference in TypeScript and writing a single data-theme attribute keeps the dark palette in exactly one place in the stylesheet, which is the property that matters: the two themes cannot disagree about a colour nobody remembered to change in both. The cost is that the theme now depends on JavaScript. For an application that is a single-page Angular bundle behind a login redirect, that dependency already existed.

Properties:
- `choice: unknown = this.choiceSignal.asReadonly()`
- `choiceSignal: unknown = signal<ThemeChoice>(storedChoice())`
- `document: unknown = inject(DOCUMENT)`
- `resolved: unknown = computed<ResolvedTheme>(() => { const choice = this.choiceSignal(); if (choice !== 'system') { return choice; } return this.systemDark() ? 'dark' : 'light'; })`
- `systemDark: unknown = signal(this.matchesDark())` — Tracked separately so a change of the OS setting repaints a system user without a reload.

Methods:
- `apply(theme: ResolvedTheme): void`
- `matchesDark(): boolean`
- `use(choice: ThemeChoice): void`
- `watchSystem(): void`

### AnswerSegment

File: `src/app/features/search/search-answer.ts`

Description: One piece of the answer text: either prose, or a citation marker that links to its source. The answer arrives with its \[P1\] markers already in the text and its claims already validated against what was retrieved. Splitting it here is presentation only — the markers become links. Nothing is re-parsed, reordered or filtered: the backend decided what the answer says, and a client that second-guessed it would be a second, weaker citation check in the place least able to make one.

Properties:
- `citation?: Citation` — For a marker: the citation it points at, when the label is one of the answer's sources.
- `kind: "text" | "marker"`
- `value: string`

### Approval

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: One protocol's approval, as PUT …/approval returns it and as every list row carries it. approvedBy and approvedAt are non-null exactly when the state is APPROVED — a database constraint says so, which is why this is a state plus its evidence rather than three independent fields the client has to reconcile.

Properties:
- `approvedAt: string | null`
- `approvedBy: string | null`
- `state: ApprovalState`

### ArchivedProtocol

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: A protocol in the archive, from GET /api/moderation/protocols/deleted . It is out of retrieval, out of every list and out of "Meine Uploads"; this is the only place it still appears. There is no restore, by design — the archive exists so that removing garbage does not also destroy the record of who produced it.

Properties:
- `deleteComment: string | null` — The stated reason. The field the whole archive exists to carry.

- `uploadedBy: string`

### Citation

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: A cited protocol. Mode A only; Mode B returns an empty list.

Properties:
- `approved: boolean` — Whether an administrator has vouched for the protocol behind this citation. On the citation rather than fetched per source, because a client that had to ask a second endpoint for it would eventually forget to — and forgetting is the failure that matters here. Unapproved protocols stay searchable by decision (2026-08-11), so a Mode A answer can be grounded in text nobody has reviewed, and NFR-2's citation discipline makes any cited claim LOOK checked. This flag is what keeps that impression honest.
- `errorCode: string | null`
- `incidentDate: string | null`
- `label: string`
- `protocolId: string`
- `similarity: number` — Cosine similarity, 0..1. Shown so the demo can say why this is Mode A and the next is Mode B.
- `title: string`

### Dictionary

File: `src/app/core/i18n/dictionary.ts`

Properties:
- `approval: { approved: string; unapproved: string; column: string; approve: string; withdraw: string; withdrawShort: string; approving: string; approvedNotice: string; wit…` — Approval: the state, and the administrator's control over it. Its own section rather than more moderation keys, because the STATE is read on three surfaces that are not the Verwaltung view — a source card under an answer, the viewer dialog, and the answer-level note — while only the verbs below belong to moderation. Splitting them by owner keeps a technician-facing word out of an admin-facing section.
- `appTagline: string`
- `appTitle: string`
- `common: { close: string; cancel: string }` — Labels that belong to no one view — the shared dialog shell reads them.
- `demo: { operator: string; techniker: string; schichtleiter: string; admin: string; examplesHeading: string; examplesIntro: string; exampleMachine: string; examples: r…`
- `duplicates: { title: string; intro: string; method: string; match: string; openCandidate: string; more: string }` — Duplicate detection, shown before an approval when the corpus already holds something close. The wording is the feature. Every string here is written to inform rather than to accuse: no "warning", no "problem", no "are you sure". The approve button in this dialog is enabled the whole time, and the text has to match — a sentence that implies wrongdoing beside a button that works anyway teaches the reader to distrust one of the two. Four legitimate E-47 protocols on one machine are the reason: being similar is normal in this corpus.
- `errors: { rateLimited: string; budgetExhausted: string; unavailable: string; forbidden: string; documentMissing: string; uploadTooLarge: string; uploadRejected: string;…`
- `footer: { docs: string; repo: string; aiUsage: string; note: string; serverUp: string; serverDown: string; serverUnknown: string }`
- `help: { title: string; modesHeading: string; modeAHeading: string; modeABody: string; modeBHeading: string; modeBBody: string; rolesHeading: string; roleOperator: str…`
- `landing: { headline: string; problem: string; solution: string; trustHeading: string; trustSourced: string; trustSourcedBody: string; trustEu: string; trustEuBody: strin…`

- `modeB: { badge: string; explanation: string; tip: string; steps: string }`
- `moderation: { heading: string; intro: string; headingCorrector: string; introCorrector: string; editResetsApproval: string; uploadedBy: string; actions: string; open: strin…` — The Protokollverwaltung view. The key stays moderation on purpose. The user-visible name changed because "Verwaltung" and "Moderation" read like a discussion forum rather than like a maintenance record; the API paths ( /api/moderation/\*\* ), the component and this key did not, because renaming an identifier to follow a label churns the tests and the wire contract for something no user can see.
- `nav: { search: string; upload: string; moderation: string; corrections: string; signOut: string; language: string; help: string; menu: string }`
- `pager: { label: string; previous: string; next: string; pageOf: string }` — The paging control, shared by the three tables that have one. Its own section rather than a copy under each view: the labels are the control's, not the table's, and three copies of "Nächste Seite" is three chances for them to drift apart.
- `roles: { operator: string; techniker: string; schichtleiter: string; admin: string }`
- `search: { heading: string; machine: string; machinePlaceholder: string; question: string; questionPlaceholder: string; submit: string; working: string; workingHint: str…`
- `settings: { title: string; open: string; aboutHeading: string; app: string; version: string; accountHeading: string; user: string; signedInSince: string; fontHeading: str…` — The gear dialog: what this is, who is signed in, and how large to draw it.
- `signOut: { title: string; body: string; notice: string; dismiss: string }`
- `theme: { label: string; light: string; dark: string }` — The theme control. Two states; the operating system is the silent default, not a button.
- `upload: { heading: string; intro: string; inputMode: string; modeFile: string; modeText: string; file: string; text: string; textHint: string; textPlaceholder: string; …`
- `viewer: { title: string; loading: string; download: string; fallbackNote: string; historyHeading: string; historyEdited: string; historyApproved: string; historyUnappro…`

### HealthStatus

File: `src/app/core/api/api.types.ts`

Description: What GET /api/health answers. Public by design (see HealthController ): it is what a load balancer, the compose healthcheck and a recruiter clicking the demo URL hit first, and none of them hold a token. version is the BACKEND's version, and nothing reads it yet — the footer indicator uses only status . It is typed here because it is part of the response, not because this PR shows it: the Settings dialog shows the FRONTEND version from package.json, and putting two different versions on screen in one release is how a reader learns to distrust both.
